ROOT Tutorial II

Code language: PyROOT · ROOT C++

Store detector measurements event by event, inspect the resulting TTree, and construct spectra and selections from the stored quantities.

Read Tutorial I first. This tutorial prepares the TTree operations used in assignment 4.1 and assignment 5.1.

Run the cells in order in a PyROOT notebook. Choose one language version; the two versions use the same examples and file format.

0. Start ROOT in Python¶

Run the notebook from the first cell to the last. Several later cells open files produced by earlier cells. Restarting the kernel clears Python variables but does not delete ROOT files already written to disk.

import numpy as np
import math
import ROOT

print("ROOT version:", ROOT.gROOT.GetVersion())

ROOT version: 6.40.00

ROOT provides the PyROOT interface. NumPy supplies small arrays whose values are copied into the primitive branches when an event is written. math supplies square roots for the simplified detector-resolution model.

%jsroot on enables interactive ROOT canvases for zooming and bin inspection. It is a Jupyter command, not ordinary Python. Older installations without this command use their configured canvas display.

%jsroot on

JSROOT interactive graphics enabled.

c1 = ROOT.TCanvas("c1_t2_py", "ROOT Tutorial II - PyROOT", 850, 650)

The same canvas is reused below. Its size and the Draw() calls work as in Tutorial I.

1. Events, entries, and branches¶

A detector system records several quantities produced by the same incident particle. Those quantities must remain associated during analysis. We call the complete record for one incident particle an event.

A TTree stores many events with a repeated structure. One stored event is normally one entry. A branch stores one field of every entry, such as the event number or a detector signal. Reading entry 25 loads the values belonging to event 25 across all branches; it does not read the 25th value from only one branch.

A tree is therefore not a histogram. A histogram accumulates bin counts and normally discards the individual input values. A tree retains event-level values so that new observables and selections can be constructed later.

The telescope event used here¶

Suppose a mixed light-ion sample containing p, d, t, ³He, ⁴He, and ⁶He is incident on a thin silicon ΔE detector followed by a sufficiently thick stopping E detector. The first detector measures signal[0], and the second measures the remaining energy as signal[1]. Both values belong to the same particle and must therefore be stored in the same tree entry.

Each simulated entry contains:

  • eventID: the sequential event number;
  • A, Z: the generated particle mass and charge numbers;
  • E0: the generated incident kinetic energy in MeV;
  • signal[0]: measured energy loss in the thin detector, in MeV;
  • signal[1]: measured energy in the thick detector, in MeV.

The generated pairs (A, Z) = (1, 1), (2, 1), (3, 1), (3, 2), (4, 2), (6, 2) correspond respectively to p, d, t, ³He, ⁴He, and ⁶He. A, Z, and E0 are simulation truth. They make it possible to check the example, but ordinary experimental data do not reveal them automatically. Event selection later in the tutorial will use measured signals rather than truth labels.

Illustrative telescope data

Generate a simple two-detector dataset for the TTree examples. The non-relativistic trend \(dE/dx\propto Z^2/v^2\), with \(v^2\propto E_0/A\), motivates the illustrative response

$$\Delta E_{\rm true}=K\frac{Z^2 A}{E_0},\qquad E_{\rm true}=E_0-\Delta E_{\rm true},$$

with \(K=8\) MeV² and \(20\le E_0\le80\) MeV. Assume the second detector stops the particle, then add Gaussian measurement fluctuations to the two signals. The parameters below are chosen for this example, not obtained from a detector calibration. Assignment 4.1 uses the three-layer energy deposits already calculated in assignment 1.2.

2. Create and fill a TTree¶

Open an output file first, then create the tree while that file is the current ROOT directory. The tree will be written to the file after all entries have been filled.

fout = ROOT.TFile("tree_telescope_python.root", "RECREATE")
tree_out = ROOT.TTree("telescope", "two-detector charged-particle telescope events")

eventID = np.zeros(1, dtype=np.int32)
A = np.zeros(1, dtype=np.int32)
Z = np.zeros(1, dtype=np.int32)
E0 = np.zeros(1, dtype=np.float32)
signal = np.zeros(2, dtype=np.float32)

TFile(filename, mode) creates or opens a ROOT file. RECREATE creates a new file and overwrites an existing file with the same name. Use it only for an output file that may safely be replaced.

TTree(name, title) creates an initially empty tree. telescope is the internal object name used by Get() later; the title is a human-readable description.

A primitive branch reads its value from an array at a stable memory location. np.zeros(1, dtype=np.int32) creates a one-element array of 32-bit signed integers; np.zeros(1, dtype=np.float32) creates a one-element array of 32-bit floating-point numbers. The first argument is the array length, and all elements start at zero. The value of a scalar branch is assigned to element 0. signal has two elements for the two detector signals. Update these arrays in place before each Fill(); keep the same array objects after calling Branch(). Each call to Fill() copies the current values into a new tree entry.

tree_out.Branch("eventID", eventID, "eventID/I")
tree_out.Branch("A", A, "A/I")
tree_out.Branch("Z", Z, "Z/I")
tree_out.Branch("E0", E0, "E0/F")
tree_out.Branch("signal", signal, "signal[2]/F")

The primitive-branch form used above is

tree.Branch(branch_name, memory_buffer, leaf_description)

The first argument is the branch name stored in the file. The second is the buffer whose current value ROOT will copy when Fill() is called. The third is a leaf list: the text before / is the leaf name, while the letter after / specifies the stored type. /I means a 32-bit signed integer and /F means a 32-bit floating-point value. In signal[2]/F, [2] declares exactly two floating-point elements per entry.

The buffer type and leaf-list type must agree. For example, pairing np.float32 with /I would cause the same memory bytes to be interpreted as the wrong type. ROOT does not infer physical units; units must be documented in names, titles, or accompanying text.

rng = ROOT.TRandom3(2026)
n_events = 60000
K_loss = 8.0  # effective constant in MeV^2

species_A = (1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 6)
species_Z = (1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2)

For each particle, update the labels, incident energy, and both signals, then call Fill() once. The entry stores these values together.

for i in range(n_events):
    eventID[0] = i

    species_index = int(rng.Integer(6))
    A[0] = species_A[species_index]
    Z[0] = species_Z[species_index]

    E0[0] = rng.Uniform(20.0, 80.0)
    dE_true = K_loss * Z[0]**2 * A[0] / E0[0]
    E_true = E0[0] - dE_true

    sigma_dE = 0.03 + 0.04 * math.sqrt(dE_true)
    sigma_E = 0.08 + 0.015 * math.sqrt(E_true)

    signal[0] = max(0.0, rng.Gaus(dE_true, sigma_dE))
    signal[1] = max(0.0, rng.Gaus(E_true, sigma_E))

    tree_out.Fill()

print("Entries held in memory:", tree_out.GetEntries())

Entries held in memory: 60000

Integer(6) chooses one of the six isotope entries with equal probability. Gaus(mean, sigma) gives a measured signal; the two sigma expressions are assumptions of this illustrative model. Fill() copies the current branch buffers into the next entry. Keep the buffers themselves in place and update their values.

fout.cd()
tree_out.Write()
fout.Close()

print("Created tree_telescope_python.root")

Created tree_telescope_python.root

fout.cd() makes the output file the current ROOT directory. Write() serializes the tree, including its branch structure and filled entries. Close() completes the file and releases the file handle. Calling Fill() alone changes the in-memory tree; it does not guarantee that the tree has been saved to disk.

3. Reopen and inspect the tree¶

Inspection should precede analysis whenever a ROOT file is unfamiliar. Confirm the file contents, tree name, branch names, branch types, array dimensions, and number of entries before writing a long event loop.

fin = ROOT.TFile.Open("tree_telescope_python.root", "READ")
fin.ls()
tree_in = fin.Get("telescope")

TFile**		tree_telescope_python.root
 TFile*		tree_telescope_python.root
  KEY: TTree	telescope;1	two-detector charged-particle telescope events

ls() lists the objects in the file. Retrieve the tree using its stored name, telescope, and keep the input file open during analysis. If the file or tree is missing, check the filename and object listing before proceeding.

tree_in.Print()
print("Number of entries:", tree_in.GetEntries())

Print() shows the entry count, branch names, types, and dimensions. Here signal[2]/F means two Float_t values in each entry. GetEntries() returns the total number of entries.

tree_in.Show(10)

======> EVENT:10
 eventID         = 10
 A               = 2
 Z               = 1
 E0              = 71.276
 signal          = 0.266728,
                  71.1437

Show(entry_number) prints all branches for one entry. Entry numbering starts at zero, so Show(10) displays the eleventh stored event. It is a diagnostic display, not a method for extracting an analysis result.

tree_in.Scan(
    "eventID:A:Z:E0:signal[0]:signal[1]",
    "",
    "",
    10,
    0,
)

************************************************************************************

************************************************************************************
*        0 *         0 *         2 *         1 * 65.996543 * 0.2959895 * 65.936271 *
*        1 *         1 *         6 *         2 * 25.333940 * 7.5492363 * 17.606323 *
*        2 *         2 *         6 *         2 * 57.311428 * 3.4103038 * 54.082107 *
*        3 *         3 *         2 *         1 * 53.495006 * 0.3692665 * 53.215637 *

*        9 *         9 *         2 *         1 * 24.489458 * 0.6236841 * 23.949422 *
************************************************************************************

The form used here is Scan(expression, selection, option, number, first_entry). Colons separate displayed expressions. Empty selection and option strings request no cut and the default format. The last two arguments show ten entries beginning at entry zero. Scan() is useful for checking a small sample; printing thousands of entries is neither an efficient analysis nor an effective validation.

4. Quick analysis with TTree.Draw()¶

Draw() lets ROOT loop over entries internally. Its main form is

tree.Draw(expression, selection, drawing_option)

The expression specifies what is plotted, the selection specifies which entries are accepted, and the drawing option controls the display. This is well suited to checking branches, exploring correlations, and testing a simple cut before writing a longer loop.

c1.Clear()
tree_in.Draw("signal[1]")
c1.Draw()

With only a branch expression, ROOT creates and displays a temporary histogram. signal[1] selects the thick-detector value from the two-element branch. The automatic range and binning are useful for inspection but should not be treated as an analysis choice.

hEres_quick_py = ROOT.TH1F(
    "hEres_quick_py",
    "Thick-detector energy;E (MeV);Counts per 0.5 MeV",
    170, 0.0, 85.0,
)

tree_in.Draw("signal[1]>>hEres_quick_py", "", "goff")
c1.Clear()
hEres_quick_py.Draw()
c1.Draw()

The histogram constructor sets 170 bins from 0 to 85 MeV, giving a 0.5-MeV bin width. In expression>>histogram_name, >> tells TTree.Draw() to fill an existing named histogram. The branch expression supplies one value per accepted entry. The option goff performs the loop without drawing immediately; the histogram is then drawn explicitly. Repeating the command resets the histogram before filling. Use >>+histogram_name only when deliberate accumulation is required.

tree_in.SetAlias("Etot", "signal[0]+signal[1]")
hEtot_quick_py = ROOT.TH1F(
    "hEtot_quick_py",
    "Reconstructed total energy;#DeltaE + E (MeV);Counts per 0.5 MeV",
    170, 0.0, 85.0,
)

tree_in.Draw("Etot>>hEtot_quick_py", "", "goff")
c1.Clear()
hEtot_quick_py.Draw()
c1.Draw()

SetAlias("Etot", "signal[0]+signal[1]") gives a short name to an expression for subsequent Draw() calls; it does not create a stored branch. Here \(E_{\rm total}=\Delta E+E\) should be close to the generated \(E_0\), apart from measurement fluctuations.

hPID_quick_py = ROOT.TH2F(
    "hPID_quick_py",
    "Charged-particle telescope response;E (MeV);#DeltaE (MeV)",
    680, 0.0, 85.0,
    440, 0.0, 11.0,
)

tree_in.Draw("signal[0]:signal[1]>>hPID_quick_py", "", "COLZ")
c1.Draw()

TTree.Draw uses y:x: signal[0] is on the y axis, signal[1] on x. The TH2F constructor lists x bins first, then y bins. COLZ displays the count in each bin by colour. The six bands come from the different isotope responses in the generated data.

helium_like_cut_py = "signal[0] > 2.5 - 0.025*signal[1]"

hPID_cut_py = ROOT.TH2F(
    "hPID_cut_py",
    "He-like events above a linear cut;E (MeV);#DeltaE (MeV)",
    680, 0.0, 85.0,
    440, 0.0, 11.0,
)

n_selected_quick_py = tree_in.Draw(
    "signal[0]:signal[1]>>hPID_cut_py",
    helium_like_cut_py,
    "COLZ",
)

h_he_boundary_py = ROOT.TLine(0.0, 2.5, 85.0, 0.375)
h_he_boundary_py.SetLineColor(ROOT.kRed + 1)
h_he_boundary_py.SetLineWidth(2)
h_he_boundary_py.Draw("SAME")
print("He-like selected entries with TTree.Draw():", n_selected_quick_py)
c1.Draw()

He-like selected entries with TTree.Draw(): 29815

The selection string accepts entries above \(\Delta E=2.5-0.025E\), approximately separating the helium bands from the hydrogen bands in this example. TLine draws the boundary; it does not perform the selection. The cut fills a selected histogram without removing any source-tree entries.

hZ_check_py = ROOT.TH1F(
    "hZ_check_py",
    "Generated Z after the linear H/He cut;Z;Entries",
    2, 0.5, 2.5,
)

tree_in.Draw("Z>>hZ_check_py", helium_like_cut_py, "goff")
c1.Clear()
hZ_check_py.Draw()
c1.Draw()

The selected histogram is dominated by Z=2. Because the simulation records particle labels, the cut can be checked against them. To inspect one isotope directly, use a selection such as "A==4 && Z==2". && means that both conditions must hold, including in a PyROOT Draw string. Assignment 4.1 uses these labels to identify the PID projection peaks.

5. Read events explicitly in PyROOT¶

TTree.Draw() is concise, but an explicit event loop is clearer when the analysis requires several derived quantities, nested conditions, counters, detector corrections, or calculations that are awkward to express as strings.

PyROOT supports direct iteration:

for event in tree:
    value = event.branch_name

During each iteration, event is a PyROOT proxy for the current tree entry. A scalar branch is accessed as an attribute, while the fixed array branch is indexed.

for i, event in enumerate(tree_in):
    print(
        int(event.eventID),
        int(event.A),
        int(event.Z),
        float(event.signal[0]),
        float(event.signal[1]),
    )
    if i == 4:
        break

0 2 1 0.2959895730018616 65.93627166748047
1 6 2 7.549236297607422 17.6063232421875
2 6 2 3.410303831100464 54.08210754394531
3 2 1 0.3692665994167328 53.21563720703125
4 4 2 3.301480770111084 35.070316314697266

The loop stops after five entries only to inspect the access syntax. int() and float() convert ROOT scalar proxies to ordinary Python values for predictable printing. They are not required when passing numeric branch values directly to ROOT histogram methods.

hEtot_loop_py = ROOT.TH1F(
    "hEtot_loop_py",
    "Total energy from explicit loop;#DeltaE + E (MeV);Counts per 0.5 MeV",
    170, 0.0, 85.0,
)
hPID_loop_py = ROOT.TH2F(
    "hPID_loop_py",
    "Telescope response from explicit loop;E (MeV);#DeltaE (MeV)",
    680, 0.0, 85.0,
    440, 0.0, 11.0,
)
hSelected_loop_py = ROOT.TH1F(
    "hSelected_loop_py",
    "Thick-detector energy for He-like events;E (MeV);Counts per 0.5 MeV",
    170, 0.0, 85.0,
)

Now read one entry at a time. Fill all derived histograms from that same entry and count those passing the selection.

selected_entries = 0

for event in tree_in:
    dE_measured = float(event.signal[0])
    E_measured = float(event.signal[1])
    E_total = dE_measured + E_measured

    hEtot_loop_py.Fill(E_total)
    hPID_loop_py.Fill(E_measured, dE_measured)

    dE_boundary = 2.5 - 0.025 * E_measured
    if dE_measured > dE_boundary:
        hSelected_loop_py.Fill(E_measured)
        selected_entries += 1

print("He-like selected entries:", selected_entries)

He-like selected entries: 29815

One entry supplies one matched pair of detector signals. The two-dimensional histogram must therefore be filled inside the same iteration with Fill(E_measured, dE_measured). Combining values from different entries would destroy the event correlation.

The loop also constructs a new observable and evaluates the same linear boundary used in TTree.Draw(). Agreement between the quick and explicit selected counts is a useful code check. The explicit loop is longer, but the calculation and selection are now normal Python expressions rather than text interpreted by ROOT.

c2 = ROOT.TCanvas("c2_t2_py", "Explicit PyROOT event loop", 1000, 450)
c2.Divide(2, 1)
c2.cd(1)
hEtot_loop_py.Draw()
c2.cd(2)
hPID_loop_py.Draw("COLZ")
h_he_boundary_py.Draw("SAME")
c2.Draw()

Divide(2, 1) creates two horizontal pads. cd(1) and cd(2) select the pad receiving the next drawing command. The first panel shows the derived total energy; the second verifies that the explicit loop preserves the two-signal event structure.

c1.Clear()
hSelected_loop_py.Draw()
c1.Draw()

Index-based access with GetEntry()¶

Direct iteration is usually the clearest PyROOT form. ROOT also supports index-based access. GetEntry(i) loads entry i into the tree object, after which branches can be read as tree.branch. This form is useful when entry indices matter or when translating an established C++ loop.

for i in range(3):
    bytes_read = tree_in.GetEntry(i)
    print(
        "entry", i,
        "bytes", bytes_read,
        "eventID", int(tree_in.eventID),
        "dE", float(tree_in.signal[0]),
        "E", float(tree_in.signal[1]),
    )

entry 0 bytes 24 eventID 0 dE 0.2959895730018616 E 65.93627166748047
entry 1 bytes 24 eventID 1 dE 7.549236297607422 E 17.6063232421875
entry 2 bytes 24 eventID 2 dE 3.410303831100464 E 54.08210754394531

GetEntry() returns the number of bytes read for that entry; it does not return the event itself. A non-positive return value indicates that no entry data were read. In ordinary PyROOT scalar analysis, explicit SetBranchAddress() calls are unnecessary because PyROOT exposes branches as attributes. The C++ notebook demonstrates the buffer-based SetBranchAddress() pattern used in compiled code.

6. Save analysis products¶

An analysis usually keeps the original event tree unchanged and writes derived histograms to a separate file. This preserves a clean distinction between input data and analysis products.

fanalysis = ROOT.TFile("telescope_analysis_python.root", "RECREATE")
fanalysis.cd()

hEtot_loop_py.Write()
hPID_loop_py.Write()
hSelected_loop_py.Write()

fanalysis.Close()
print("Created telescope_analysis_python.root")

Created telescope_analysis_python.root

The output file contains derived histograms, while tree_telescope_python.root remains the event-level input. Calling Write() explicitly avoids ambiguity about which objects should become persistent. The original tree need not be copied into every analysis file.

7. Fixed arrays in the assignments

The same branch pattern stores detector energies or waveform samples:

DataLeaf descriptionOne entry
This examplesignal[2]/FTwo detector signals
Assignment 4.1e[3]/F, A/I, Z/ID1, D2, D3 energy deposits and the particle labels
Assignment 5.1adc[250]/D in tree wave250 samples of one pulse

/F is Float_t, /D is Double_t, and /I is Int_t. The array type and length in memory must match the file.

For a waveform, GetEntry(i) loads the whole pulse. An inner loop over the array then calculates its baseline or charge integral. The next GetEntry replaces the buffer contents with the next pulse.

PyROOT also supports the C++ buffer-reading pattern. For the signal branch already used above:

signal_read = np.zeros(2, dtype=np.float32)
tree_in.SetBranchAddress("signal", signal_read)
tree_in.GetEntry(0)
print("First event signals:", signal_read[0], signal_read[1])
tree_in.ResetBranchAddresses()

First event signals: 0.29598957 65.93627

SetBranchAddress connects the array to the branch; GetEntry fills it. ResetBranchAddresses releases that connection when finished. For adc[250]/D, use an array of 250 np.float64 values instead.

fin.Close()

Summary

Branch defines the stored fields; Fill writes one event; Write saves the tree. Read Print before choosing branch names and array indices. Use Draw for expressions and selections, or GetEntry for calculations on individual events. Quantities used together always come from the same entry.
